report:
## What the evidence shows

The claim that ginkgo biloba extract relieves tinnitus is **not well supported by rigorous evidence**, despite being widely believed and marketed.

**Cochrane review (highest-quality evidence):** The Cochrane Database systematic review of ginkgo biloba for tinnitus found only a few good-quality trials (four studies, ~1,543 participants) and concluded there is **no reliable evidence that ginkgo reduces tinnitus severity compared to placebo** (https://www.cochrane.org/hr/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus).

**Individual RCTs are mixed and mostly negative.** Some older, smaller trials (e.g., Rejali et al., and Morgenstern/Biesinger's EGb 761 study) reported modest benefit, but larger, well-designed placebo-controlled trials — most notably one described as "Ginkgo biloba does not benefit patients with tinnitus" combined with a meta-analysis of randomized trials — found no significant effect (https://www.tinnitusjournal.com/articles/ginkgo-biloba-in-the-treatment-of-tinnitus-an-updated-literature-review.html). A 2011 systematic review similarly found inconsistent, generally weak results (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/).

**Clinical guidelines agree.** The American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS) 2014 Clinical Practice Guideline on Tinnitus explicitly **recommends against** using ginkgo biloba (along with zinc and melatonin) for tinnitus treatment, citing insufficient evidence of benefit (https://scispace.com/pdf/clinical-practice-guideline-tinnitus-3ptl4asefl.pdf).

## Bottom line
Your sister's belief reflects popular assumption and some older small studies with positive results, but the strongest, most rigorous evidence—Cochrane's systematic review and major clinical guidelines—concludes ginkgo does not reliably relieve tinnitus symptoms beyond placebo. It's generally low-risk to try, but current science does not support it as an effective treatment.
